page_title: The Audit Log Wall of Shame

sources.entry: The Audit Log Wall of Shame: list of vendors that don’t prioritize high-quality, widely-available audit logs for security and operations teams.

summary.title: The Audit Log Wall of Shame
summary.one_liner: A community-maintained list of SaaS and infrastructure vendors whose audit logs are gated, incomplete, or poorly formatted, plus a framework for judging what makes an audit log good for security teams.
keywords: what makes a good audit log
takeaways: Audit logs record a historical, immutable record of activity for compliance and policy enforcement, unlike system logs used for troubleshooting.
Many vendors gate detailed audit logs behind higher pricing tiers, extra SKUs, or usage-based billing.
Good audit logs include source IPs, user attribution, consistent UTC timestamps, documented event types, and old/new values for changes.
Good log collection supports streaming to cloud storage or a SIEM, sortable event IDs to avoid gaps or duplicates, and consistent structure across versions.
summary.summary: The page is a list of vendors (such as 1Password, AWS CloudTrail, GitHub, GitLab, LastPass, Salesforce, and Slack) with the gating mechanism for their audit logs and specific log issues found for each. It opens with a definition of audit logs versus system logs and explains why defenders depend on vendor-provided audit data. The second half sets out criteria for a good audit log across content, collection, and quality/consistency, along with examples of bad log design such as unordered arrays in nested JSON and inconsistent field names. The page invites community edits through its GitHub repository.
